title: ADHD Mind-Training Game
body:
I'm an adult, over 40. I've struggled hard with ADHD, mixed with some obsessive compulsive tendencies. I've been using the game regularly, but not daily, for a couple of weeks. I believe it is helping. I've been trying to incorporate playing it into my day, like ... 5-20 minute of mind therapy (comparable to physical therapy for the body) or high speed meditation? Your experience may vary. 

The concept is fairly simple, guiding an avatar, surfing along in the water. Click when you see the target object swoosh by, while either aiming for, or avoiding items in your path. 

Now, there are some places I feel it should improve. My overall feeling about the effect of the app is good. My comments are to praise what works, and suggest tweaks.

Graphics are cute, but geared toward kids. The scenes are pretty, though you can't stop to look. The concept of cruising along an endless water surface is a pleasant one. Surfing in the sunshine. I like the default avatar, but you can change their appearance. 

When it comes to the bird guides, the graphic style is different. I think they are trying for a Monument Valley look (great puzzle game BTW), but it's not quite there. For me they are a little creepy, but that may be sour grapes, because the guides sometimes speed up the journey and make it even harder for a few seconds. 

I wish the game would give you a little time to get good at it just for a couple of sessions. Naturally, it gets harder as you go, to train your mind to focus on a goal, while still handling "moving along in life." But, just a couple sessions of having mastered it would make it less irritating as it gets more difficult. It's painful to feel you're bad and will always fail. I already constantly fail, that's why I'm trying this app to improve my focus and avoid distraction. Slightly less painful with the sound effects off, I find. I've had to take the attitude of "who cares, it's just a game. I'm doing it for my long-term benefit." But if I do it at the end of a day where I've failed to get much done... you can see where it would be discouraging.

Also, if you miss a target object, the avatar turns around to watch it go past, which makes it harder to focus on the next target. The avatar getting distracted is really annoying.

Overall, would recommend. It's still early days. Will try to post new thoughts, if any.

title: Expensive, No Trial and Out of Touch with ADHD users
body:
I’m honestly disappointed with EndeavorOTC.

This is an app marketed to people with ADHD and priced at a premium, yet there’s no meaningful trial period. That makes very little sense for this audience. Many people with ADHD struggle with consistency and often start tools with the best intentions, only to find after a short time that they don’t stick. Asking for a high upfront commitment without the chance to properly test whether it actually works for you feels out of touch with the realities of ADHD.

Being FDA-cleared is not a justification for pharmaceutical-level pricing, especially for a digital product with minimal marginal cost. FDA clearance speaks to safety and evidence, not to whether the product should be priced in a way that limits access.

The combination of high cost and no trial makes me question the priorities behind this app. It’s hard not to wonder whether the focus is truly on helping people with ADHD, or on maximizing revenue from a vulnerable group. Supporting users and running a business are not mutually exclusive, but the current approach feels like a clear choice about which comes first.

title: Great adjunct treatment tool
body:
I’ve used EndeavorOTC for about three months now. It noticeably helps me stay focused and more even-keeled. Some notes on the game:

- the basic gameplay is to tilt your phone to maneuver through power boosts or around obstacles while also tapping when target objects appear. The speed adjusts over the course of level based on your performance. Most levels have a guide that leads the way (usually a bird) and the more you succeed in your task, the closer you get to your guide. The levels ends when you “capture” the guide with improved game play or run out of time. 

- It’s not an overnight treatment. For me, it took about a month before I noticed effects, and about six weeks before I hit a long plateau and really started working. Still, at 10-15 minutes a day, it hasn’t been hard to keep up with

- The game play is different from non-therapeutic video games. You can’t choose the difficulty of the level (although you can choose the type of level once you reach expert mode) and the selected targets change with every round. The game also seems to detect if a player is taking shortcuts, I.e. if I try to get two power boosts by skipping a different more difficult one in between, the level tends to slow down pretty dramatically. 

-Traditional video games also come with a lot of prizes, consequences, and media effects to build a sense of urgency. (E.g. getting a lot of boosts in a row will give you a combo with flashing color changes and an increasing multiplier.) This game has far more subtle cues when you have successes or misses, and there’s no score or health bar visible while you’re playing. Players can’t rely on the same kinds of adrenaline or dopamine rushes to pull them through. 

- the support team was very responsive when I had minor issues with lag, which resolved after apple released a new iPhone update. 

- I’ve found this app works well in combo with meditation apps. Practicing the process of recognizing thoughts that arise and releasing them is useful for recognizing targets on screen and then quickly reorienting to steering through boosts and obstacle.

title: Controls and Positioning make playing incomfortable
body:
I am the art lead at a game design studio, and I heard about this app through an article. I was very excited to try it out, since I have ADHD. I really like the idea, and it did force me to focus a lot. But there are some problems with how the game functions.

First off, you have to hold your device flat, which means that you're uncomfortably craning over- that in itself is quite distracting, and doesn't seem necessary since there are so many racing games where the device can be held vertically. If there is a specific reason that it needs to be held flat, then that should be mentioned (neurological, focus?). If not, it's a pretty big design flaw and should probably be adjusted.

Secondly, the experience is surprisingly OK on an iPad, but not on an iPhone. The touch areas on the left and right get obscured by your thumbs, so sometimes you can't see the target spheres flying at you and miss them.

Finally, I found the actual tilt control to be overly sensitive, and the interaction boundary that you crash into extends past the actual edge mesh. Many times, I was punished for hitting the side of the path, when I very clearly didn't. There might be a consistent boundary set along there instead of a mesh-based collider, that would be my guess. 

I also have worked on edutainment games, so something like this is extremely exciting. It's only in early access, but these are the big three gameplay things I would try to improve. (As well as not forcing somebody to spend $25 to try a month for EA- there is no free trial available that I could find. I know game development is expensive, but that's too much.)

body:

One of my biggest struggles with ADHD is executive disfunction and all the extra time it takes me to start and complete tasks due to all my dilly dallying, committing to this treatment plan has cut down that time DRASTICALLY as well as all of the anxiety and depression that used to result from the struggle. Now I just plan something and I do the thing? I feel so efficient and my confidence has significantly improved. Bonus tip: if you meditate or have a brief period of non-sleep deep rest within four hours of a session (or any kind of study session) it helps your brain to really rewire all of those changes in your brain aka it makes your brain a better sponge for everything you are learning.

***UPDATE*** 
After having this app for almost a year I will not be renewing it or recommending it to anyone. Once all of the levels are unlocked there is no further skill development other than the game getting faster and faster in order to further challenge the user. There is not enough variety in the levels, you are just supposed to play them over and over. All of the positive effects I had noticed in the beginning eventually plateaued.

title: Evidence lacking - please read - misleading studies
body:

However, the evidence they cite is very shaky if you dig into it. 
For example, consider “STARS-ADHD” study. It has no control! They enroll 221 adults to test the product, but did not have a control group that did not access the product. So there’s zero evidence that the change was caused by the product. 

It’s really misleading. It raises the serious question of why there was no control group. 

My personal experience is that I used this app daily for 6 weeks and I can’t say I felt an improvement in my attention.

title: Just a bad game, don’t download
body:
TLDR; This is not a treatment for ADHD/ADD, it’s just a bad game. The research backing this is weak at best. Rich people made this to get richer by accessing your health insurance money.

This game requires an actual medical care provider to prescribe it to you because it takes advantage of a legal loophole that was put in place during the COVID-19 pandemic to allow companies to access health coverage to experiment with apps and devices aid in Telehealth communications and other remote health care to aid in the global health crisis. This app is not FDA approved or certified as a treatment for ADHD. Read the fine print for details. Also take a look at the Terms of Use and Privacy policy as you may be divulging more data than you may be comfortable with.

This game only addresses one small facet of a multifaceted mental health issue, FOCUS. They measure the success of the product by whether or not individuals were able to focus on the game for a bit. Their only “research” was testing a group of only about 200 people of which only about half mentioned that their focus had changed while playing the game. As others have pointed out, any video game will do this. Other games will do a better job of stimulating the brain, improving skills, and engaging the user in meaningful activity. 

This game is repetitive, boring, clunky, and ugly. The points don’t mean anything. You will not gain any new skills from this game. This game is not an appropriate substitute for ADHD medication or counseling, nor is it even an appropriate addition to the many tools out there for treating ADHD.

DO NOT under any circumstances use this as the only treatment for ADHD. 

It’s the equivalent of telling a starving person to go eat some air. Will it fill your stomach? Maybe a little? Will some people tell you it works? Absolutely. Will it actually work? Of course it won’t.

title: Fun and engaging
body:

I think there’s also room to explore other games, but I think the baseline gameplay challenge needs to be super smooth. Like Super Mario is popular for both casual players and speed running because the gameplay is both accessible but also *feels* nice to play so you can grind away at it. My impression is EndeavorOTC works by getting me into flow state playing a continuous attention/motion game, while still requiring me to pay attention for quick visual pattern recognition. I think the pattern matching challenge is fine, except it’s hard to watch for patterns on a tiny screen while I’m physically shaking my phone around and need to also keep my thumbs off the screen to avoid false inputs. (Games like DDR address this by being edge-triggered rather than level-triggered; you don’t get penalized for continuing to stand on a button after activating it, and high skill players rely on this.)

I’d like to be able to play with a  video game controller though. For example, let me play on tvOS using a PS5 controller. I’d have a much easier time looking at a stable screen, using a joystick to pilot, and multiple available physical buttons to press whichever is most convenient (or make it an extra difficulty at higher levels that there are separate buttons to press for different obstacles )

title: Good and bad
body:
First of all, I do feel like this game has improved my focus.  I haven’t ever been diagnosed with ADHD but I have had my struggles with focus, and I’ve noticed some little improvements over the last month of playing this.  

My main issue with this game is ergonomics. 

I’ve always been a decent gamer but I’ve never had great wrists, and the repetitive wrist motion of this phone based game has led to some carpal-tunnel-like soreness which has the unpleasant side effect of effecting my workouts at the gym and skiing.  

Unfortunately the game seems to rely on more physical movement as you progress through it, so eventually your “focus score” seems like it will directly correlate to how well you can physically perform the steering motion, which doesn’t seem to be in line with the clinical efficacy we are going for with this. 

You’ll eventually get to a point where the steering targets are basically staggered on opposite sides of the track, so you’re just constantly banking L R L R L R L for a good chunk of the time you spend on the game, and it’s far more physically taxing than mentally.

Even aside from the wrists, I haven’t really found an effective ergonomic posture for playing the game, it seems like you have to be hunched over, with arms supported on a table or something which allows the wide wrist movement required to hit the targets.  I think there’s a lot of room for improvement in this area.

title: Doesn’t really work— too many game design flaws
body:
I’ve played this very consistently for four weeks, surpassed my goal focus score, but have seen little to no improvement in my ADHD symptoms. There are numerous game design flaws, particularly with the algorithm that supposedly makes it a treatment, that undermine the treatment potential for any functional adult.

1) It is designed so that you graduate to increasingly difficult worlds as you progress. Great— except I beat all the game content in 2 weeks, and am now stuck repeating the same missions over and over— erasing the possibility of fostering neuroplasticity. 

2) The game design is lacking both creativity and detailed attention to the point of it becoming ineffective. Mainly I’m talking about the visual targets—- where color is the main differentiator it’s okay, but half the game also depends on identifying objects by shape— but some objects look similar to most others while a couple have distinct shapes— which would be fine if the algorithm that calculates your scores and modulates difficulty knew this— but it doesn’t. I can predict whether I’ll pass a mission and whether my “selectivity” and “reaction time” will be high or low based on which object is selected for that mission— if it’s one that blends in the mission becomes more difficult but the algorithm doesn’t realize this

3) The function of the algorithm is too obvious — the game speeds up and slows down in a terribly jerky fashion every time you hit several targets in a row, or miss one, respectively. 

4) It is supposed to limit you to 25 minutes a day— but the amount it subtracts from daily timer is often incorrect by a minute. The game has the gaul to scold me for playing only 22 minutes per day (the number varies) when in fact I played until the game stopped me each day consistently. It doesn’t make sense

5) Again, I’m more distracted and addicted to my phone than before i started this “treatment.” MAYBE my visual processing is a hair better. If I had never played a  video game maybe it would have caused adaptive changes … but it didn’t. 

I think the product has potential but the game feels extremely incomplete, and at best in alpha or beta testing phase. Save your money until they have competitors and game design has been completed in a couple years.

title: Meh
body:
I loaded and played this with an open, hopeful mind. I’m not a big “gamer” - neither video games or mobile app games - so I don’t have sophisticated  gameplay expectations or know about fancy features. However, i
Think a basic expectation of any game - and probably any therapeutic treatment experience - is engagement. I suppose that this game does require one to be engaged to succeed,  but it’s not an engaging game. It’s repetitive and not very exciting.
That said, I played at least 15 minutes 5 days out of the 7-day trial, and while my ability improved, my interest declined. On the second or third day, I couldn’t gain any speed and that was incredibly irritating (I’d compare it to the pixelated pace in the original Oregon Trail computer game). I’m not sure that was intentional or a glitch, but I tried to stick it out. The next day, the game moved faster again.  Another issue I noticed is that the targets (creatures) the player is supposed to ID while navigating are often too similar to differentiate when using peripheral vision. I understand this might be a purposeful part of the “treatment.”
As to the treatment, I DID appreciate the prompts throughout the game that a) reminds it’s intended to be “treatment,” and b) suggest small changes to incorporate into the player’s days.  That said, the player should be aware that according to the summary of this game, this “treatment” has then credibility of one very small and short “study” (220 people, 6 weeks). It’s unclear how participants were chosen, observed, tracked, or evaluated; further, there isn’t any explanation as to whether participants were engaged in/ receiving any other therapeutic efforts that might affect their “focus score” (which seems dubious to me). 
Finally, as far as cost goes, it seems like this l sort of app - help for ADHD, procrastination, etc - are currently trending, AND that the app creators think it reasonable to charge unreasonable rates for unfinished products. To be fair, this one is Less expensive than some of the “daily management” apps I’ve seen, but it’s still overpriced for what’s offered. I’m comparing it to a different daily digital  “treatment” I use - a VR fitness game - that recently LOWERED their subscription price to $10/month $100/yr (from $18/mo or $120/yr).  Everyday, their coaches post 2-3 new workouts of varying difficulties with different music. It’s never the same. Meaning, it’s clear that there is a consistently significant investment not only in maintaining the functionality of the “game” AND improving it/creating new content. Players aren’t navigating the same virtual course over and over. They aren’t receiving computer-generated voices saying the same 3 messages over and over.   AND the instruction they’re providing is backed by significant research and development.

I’ve only played it for a few days, but I’m already seeing a little bit of benefit. Hopefully it continues. It’s a bit expensive, but for the benefits, it’s on par with other treatments. We’ll worth it imo.  

My only suggestion is adding more cosmetics. I’m not far along, but I can already tell I’ll run out of things to spend gold on within a month or two. Maybe add more “legendary” skins, for a higher price point? Or add vehicle skins? Maybe the ability to pay some gold to have the maps (or obstacles) look different?

title: Game itself 5/5, other factors not so much
body:
(To save time, I suggest skimming the pros checklist and the first paragraph under cons)

Pros: 
-Credible data/research 
-Great design 
-Attractive visuals
-Fun to play
-25 min per day limit 

I got this app a few days ago, so can’t speak to its effectiveness quite yet but saw the research info and I have a lot of trust in its effectiveness! The evidence appears very credible and I can personally see how it would strengthen attention/focus! 

The game is actually pretty fun for a treatment modality and has a polished look. The quality of the game is higher than most mobile games, IMO. I think the landscapes are attractive in a way that would be appealing to many ADHDers and there are fun little “extras” built in that help maintain interest in continual/habitual use. I also appreciate the way the game logs gameplay time, only allowing 25 min of play per day. We tend to struggle with time blindness, pulling ourselves away from stimulating activities, and impulse control, so having this built into the game is really helpful. 

Cons
-Free trial conditions/sketchy sales strategy
-Avatars
-Limited breakdown of focus score 

My first real “beef” with this game—which is my biggest complaint—is the conditions for the free trial. In order to have any trial before buy, the app requires committing to a yearly subscription, which I believe is about $100+. Those with ADHD struggle with remembering to follow through with important tasks (ie, canceling before auto renewal) and impulsivity (ie, signing up for a high-risk free trial despite obvious and likely consequences). By not allowing a free trial with the monthly subscription, it feels like they are knowingly using this to their advantage and exploiting based on disability. This doesn’t sit right with me. I understand the main benefits come from the first ~6 weeks of treatment, so I could understand not wanting to give a whole week of this for free, but it would be nice if they could offer at least a couple-day trial with a weekly subscription. I went ahead and bought the first month, because the data appeared credible and I would pay this monthly rate for other treatments, but I don’t appreciate the bait. Especially because it seems 6weeks is the ideal trial time, so a yearly subscription seems unnecessary. Another reason the trial conditions give the company a bad look. 

The only other “cons” are quite minor—I think there could be more “mature” avatar options that would be appealing for adult players, but of course this is not a huge deal. I’d also love to see more of a breakdown on how the focus score might reflect on a symptoms screening and tell us how our symptoms might compare to non-ADHDer performance. Again, not a huge deal. 

Overall, love the treatment/game development. Despise the sales strategy.
author: Staff'am

title: Useful for ADHD; drawbacks include posture, pace
body:
You’re gonna need to complete the game with some time in “up dog” position, getting the curve out of your neck and spine. My back tightens up to get the phone to steer correctly. 

Despite the lack of ergonomics in the game design (play with screen horizontal not vertical), the game seems to be working for me. …I’m just not sure if making me better at multitasking is a great skill. I was looking to build up focus for one accomplishment, for a longer period of time. I find that after the game, I’m good at, say, calling customer service for something by phone, while also chatting with a different customer service for another thing, while toggling back and forth between websites needed for those two conversations. 
—Does that make me productive? Maybe. Does it make life feel more hectic and stressful (like in the game)? Also yes. The game has seemed to make me better at frantically moving through tasks, but not at calm, steady focus. This is a great game for someone who, say, works on an assembly line or in some kind of customer service. Not so much folks who want to write a book or study a topic.

The game makes it hard to progress from world to world. Visual cues are designed to be tough—-but honestly, they’re so tough to tell the shape of targets apart by level 2 that the game feels frustrating. Is this a rounded, diamond, or square shaped tiny alien flying across my phone in a fraction of a second? Take best guess, get punished in the game for doing it wrong.

The focus score doesn’t show up for a long time—day by day it seems to just tell you you’ve played another day. Maybe at the end of 15 days of play it’ll finally tell you your focus score?  

I’m hopeful this app will be helpful for me, giving it two months (and $50!!!!!) which seems like way too much money.

title: Great idea but makes me mad
body:
I get long winded so I’ll put the summary first. Great idea but a frustrating execution. I’m going to keep going but this game makes me mad. 

So first, I am 27 years old, I have ADHD and I play games. I am a mobile games QA Engineer, so it’s my job to test games. So when I see an app that helps ADHD by gaming I thought that sounds awesome, let’s do it! Here are my thoughts, and I’ll try to organize them as best I can but they may be scattered because ADHD. 

The game is hard. Ridiculously hard. The collision boxes on your vehicle vs the speed boosts are exact, so if you’re like me and you’re trying to steer so the jet catches the boost so you can more easily get the next one, you just missed a boost. The collision box is only on the platform your guy is standing on, so front and center hit or not at all. The creature tapping part gets to be so quick that I’ve been punished for blinking at the wrong time. I get that the game is supposed to be hard, and I love me some hard games, but I have never lost on level/world 1 as many times as I’ve lost on this game. Dark souls and Hades have nothing on the difficulty spike here, it’s kind of insane. 

Because of this, you feel like every single mistake is getting you farther away from that elusive chance to finish the level. Messages and notifications become annoyances because I need all of that screen space and I need to put my phone in airplane mode literally every time I play this game. That’s a risk of mobile gaming, but it’s one that really is intrusive. Likewise, the controls I feel like are kind of an issue. Tilting to steer is great except for when you need pinpoint precision at all times on the screen you’re constantly moving. I do appreciate that the hit box on the right button is big enough that I can tap in the general area and it count. 

Total and complete focus is a must. My wife can’t try to talk to me while I’m playing this. My pets can’t try to nuzzle me for attention. As I mentioned before, my phone is in airplane mode. Any distraction is an annoyance because it’ll result in anywhere from 1-4 misses and my chances of clearing the level are that much lower. 

All that to say…I intend to keep trying it. Even writing this I can feel my brain feeling a little different from the few minutes I spent today prior to the review. I’m a few days in and I can tell it’s doing some work. So maybe my complaints are what’s needed for improvement? I don’t know. But I do know that this game makes me mad, and I intend to keep letting it do so. 

Devs, if this review is helpful I’ve already emailed you a question to your support email. Feel free to shoot me one back, and to use it as a method of communication if I can be of any help, I’d love for gamified treatment of anything to become more of a thing.

title: No & No
body:
This was recommended by my mother who’s dedicated much of her free time and effort into researching ADHD since my diagnosis. 

However - please don’t use this app.

 Most anything specially marketed towards a medical condition that’s a non-medical product is no better than a scam. Never trust an “ADHD-[insert noun or service]”. 

This app is no different.

 Now, the research this app is based on is sound. Repeated skill building activities that challenge your brain strengthen neuropathways to increase attention duration, focus, and memory recall; true. But you shouldn’t have to pay, much less when you realize that none of this research is secular to the ADHD mind. This science works for everybody. Building these skills is beneficial to ADHD individuals AND neurotypical minds. This product isn’t a profound treatment for ADHD, it’s implicit science. 

But even with the science being reliable, the way it’s incorporated as a product is exploitative and inefficient.

 To put it in perspective, twenty minutes a day might seem helpful - surely it’s better than zero or ten minutes - but is twenty minutes a day really enough? Twelve dollars ($12) a month for twenty minutes a day (20 min); a hundred-forty minutes a week (140 min); five hundred-sixty minutes a month (560 min) - that’s little more than nine hours total each month. Which, granted, ten hours is not insignificant but imagine only allowing an athlete to train twenty minutes a day and expecting to see more than marginal improvement in a reasonable timeframe. And, yes, maybe that twenty minute limit is a way to prevent burnout but … you know what one of the best things that negates burnout is? Results; rewards and encouragement. 

What will be most helpful to an individual with ADHD is coaching and medication, both of which are costly but are much more worthwhile than leeching gimmicks. But, as an additive, free alternatives, some which still contain in-app purchases or premiums, are most often tagged as “brain games”, “mental training”, or “mindfulness” apps. My personal favorite is “Luminosity”, which is FREE with trend functions and a variety of games focused of certain skills. No payment; no time limit; no exploitation of diagnosed users. 

Don’t allow this company to prey on you and your illnesses. End.

title: Effective mental treatment — needs multi device testing for hand/thumb placement
body:
I just started playing this yesterday, and was impressed. After playing for 25 minutes, I felt mentally tired, my heart was racing, and then I proceeded to have the most productive day ever. I play a fair amount of video games, and I would say that this is very different from a regular video game in a few ways: the first is the auto adjusting difficulty level. I could tell the speed and rate of play was adjusting to push me or back off if I wasn’t doing so well. The second is that it isn’t fun in the same way a regular video game is. It’s rewarding, but it really pushes my mental focus for sustained periods of time in a way that playing normal video games does not. Regular video games are engaging, but don’t push my brain to exhaustion the way this does. I also very much appreciate that you cannot play longer than 25 minutes a day.

My one major criticism: the tapping buttons are terribly placed for phones. This has clearly been mainly tested on iPads and I’m sure the experience is better for adult hands on them. I’ve played two days on my iPhone 13 mini, and the target positioning is too low — my right thumb almost immediately started cramping on the second day of play trying to hold the phone and tap the correct button spot. I simply can not physically play to the level my brain could tolerate because my thumbs were cramping up. I imagine sustained playing of this game on a phone might lead to tendonitis if those button positions aren’t adjusted for smaller devices. That said, I think this is a relatively simply UI fix. If the buttons were moved farther up, or a wider area of the screen would register as a correct tap for smaller devices, this issue could be alleviated. I would encourage Akili to test the button positioning for a few sized adult hands on a number of different sized Apple phones, and after testing, give a couple of button position options for different sized hands and devices. I’m going to see if I can borrow an iPad to play this because the mental effects have already amazed me, I just can’t develop issues with my hands trying to treat my ADHD.

However, I’m not JUST adhd. I’m visually impaired. The app is so fast moving that I keep losing levels because I can’t see the targets fast enough to hit the button before it disappears. Most of the time you’re getting less than a second to respond to these visual stimuli. 

The graphics and theme are fun, but this could really use some more accessibility options if it’s going to work for people that struggle with button mashing, rapid hand/wrist movements or tracking moving targets visually with your eyes. 

I would happily turn off some of the visual flair if it would make this game more accessible for me to play, so I hope you add some colorblind/visual accessibility options as well as an alternative to the accelerometer for people with dexterity/strength issues. I saw some other reviews that people trying to play this on a tablet were even getting pain because of how fast it expects you to jerk the screen around. Definitely not ideal.

title: Brain Training Backed by Research!
body:
As someone who has played the game, read 80% of the research and published material, and received zero funding for this review, I urge you to consider my words, especially if you've read any previous reviews. 

As a strong advocate for mental health, I have written online articles about being late-diagnosed at 38y/o with ADHD on Alamo City Moms and am actively researching this information as part of my degree. In my opinion, this app is a game-changer for the industry of digital treatment and non-pharmaceutical options! 

Let's look at the big picture together – this game is based on the same technology used in the prescription version that both non-traditional and traditional medicine agreed on enough to pass FDA approval for children. **This kind of approval is almost unheard of!** The positive results for this technology, from my understanding, are not diagnosis-specific, which could have a great impact on Alzheimer's and dementia patients. 

Furthermore, the approval of this technology opens the door to accepting other digital or technologically advanced treatments. Although some of these treatments are available in private practices, they can cost up to 10 times more and are rarely covered by insurance. This means that the public will have access to an alternative treatment option without such significant barriers to entry, making it accessible to more people. 

Of course, there's room for improvement in the 'over the counter' version. Users providing constructive feedback can only make the game better for everyone. Some areas that need improvement include the target thumb areas, but it's not on all levels or worlds (possibly already addressed in the last update,) and the need for a game onboarding that explains different areas and their purposes within the application/game itself. However, these "issues" do not compromise the overall usability of the game or its intended purpose of brain training. 

Regarding my results, I treat playing the game consistently like lifting weights with the goal of increasing my personal record. Some days, I feel mentally strong and win quite a few rounds, while other days my brain is challenged to the point of failure and I’m questioning why I keep playing. After a bit of rest and recovery, my focus and clarity come back even stronger than before. 

But don't just take my word for it. There is enough research out there about the technology to help you form an educated opinion before you try it.

title: UI
body:
Maybe something is not quite right with how my thumb conducts electricity, or maybe my hands are small,  but I find it really easy to miss the “Target” button. I wish there was a way to customize the UI more, for example to put the target button in different places on the screen that would be more comfortable for people’s hands, or be able to make it bigger or smaller. 

Otherwise, I will keep trying. I don’t think it has made too much difference yet.
author: Disappointed SW fan

title: Great app, ridiculous rules
body: I absolutely love this app for focus training! It has been incredibly helpful in improving my concentration skills. But oh, that 25-minute/day restriction! It's honestly frustrating because I'm so passionate about it. I yearn to spend more time immersed in its engaging exercises. It's like a magnetic force pulling me in, and I can't resist! I truly wish they would consider extending the playtime because this app has become my ultimate addiction. It's just that amazing!

title: Can you read between the lines?
body:
It’s not straightforward, but start by sorting reviews by most recent so there’s no doctoring of reviews of any kind.  

Then note the ratings, user names, how they say things.  See the trend.  For positive reviews, the usernames are super random, (computer created), super Lala generic five star yay, etc.  Then read the negative reviews.  And you’ll be like dang, these guys are bad news bears.  Calling it a medical treatment when it’s not.  Using their self created promotional reviews that are not legit.  Bummer that people get so money hungry that they’ll do this kinda thing.  Somebody didn’t get swaddled as a baby.  Who knows.

title: Trying to monetize us forgetting to cancel subscriptions
body: This is not okay. It’s a video game. You practice skills just like any video game skills.  What is happening here is that this company wants to exploit your adhd by charging you to play a video game. I downloaded it and did the free trial. Then I realized, oh yeah, because I have adhd I am less likely to remember to cancel my free trial and then then this company gets $130 from me. And I will play it for a week and forget about it. This is not how this should be done. If you want to make an app for an adhd person have a cheap monthly subscription that does not auto renew. That would be an adhd friendly app. This is just mean….

title: Excited for the possibilities!
body:
I’m excited for an opportunity to improve my focus and to use my phone for something other than doom-scrolling. The research behind this looks promising and I’m looking forward to the long-term benefits! 

I actually reached out to provide feedback on the game itself and the team supporting this is very clearly excited about this product’s potential to help improve people’s lives. 

I just got into the second world and can feel my focus skills improving. The cost is far lower than any prescription medicine, so I’m very open to this new way of improving my ADHD symptoms! I’ll report back in 6 weeks (apparently the recommended time to engage with the app).
author: kswissto

title: An ADHD alternative with evidence
body: I heard about the prescription version for kids a few years ago and was disappointed there was not an option for adults. I downloaded this right away and think it’s probably better that a prescription is not required for adults since so many cannot get to a doctor for a diagnosis or treatment. I cannot take stimulants but still want to improve my focus and concentration. I’ve only been playing for a week so I can’t speak to the full benefit yet, but I read the summary of the evidence and it seems very credible. The game itself could use some design updates and better data for me to understand how I’m doing each day but otherwise it’s pretty straightforward and even fun when I get into it. I can generally understand how the challenges would improve my focus and I’m really looking forward to the results! Others have commented on the price but I guess I wouldn’t expect a treatment for ADHD to be less than $30 a month so it seems reasonable to me.
